source.title: A Simple Method for Accelerating Grokking

record.file_problem: The supplied post text includes prose referring to result graphs, but the graphs are not present; exact accuracy and step values cannot be read.
record.tranche_reason: It tests grokking on modular arithmetic using a delayed Frobenius-norm regularization method and compares it with Grokfast, rather than reproducing the original training method.
record.gate_note: The post reports a head-to-head comparison across four modular arithmetic operations and qualitative results from a hyperparameter sweep. It does not provide plotted trajectories or exact per-task accuracy or step counts in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The post proposes a way to speed up grokking: train to overfit, then add a Frobenius-norm (L2) penalty. It reports only that method's steps-to-grok against Grokfast on modular arithmetic. It does not measure whether test accuracy jumps long after training saturates, or how the delay scales with training-set size. This is method performance with grokking used as a tool, so no version is tested. Plots are absent and no numbers are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author also claims (TL;DR) grokking in roughly half Grokfast's steps. The author says the method seems to beat or match Grokfast after tuning, but expresses doubt that something is being missed.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a delayed compression schedule: after training accuracy reaches 99%, adds a Frobenius-norm penalty. The post also compares against Grokfast using the Grokfast authors' codebase.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative results change across modular operations; the post reports a separate hyperparameter sweep and says the best-settings comparison differs from the initial run.

fits_no_version.finding: Applying an L2/Frobenius penalty only after training accuracy reaches 99% leads to grokking within about 2,000 steps on modular arithmetic. The post reports this as roughly half Grokfast's steps, with instability or forgetting afterwards. It also notes, anecdotally, about 40,000 steps to grok without weight decay versus about 2,000 with it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A norm penalty applied only after memorization is enough to trigger fast generalization on algorithmic tasks, so the timing of grokking is controlled by when low-norm pressure is applied.

record.problems: The supplied text omits the referenced plots and gives no exact step counts, accuracy values, seed count, or uncertainty estimates. Model details and training-set size are not stated. The author notes catastrophic forgetting and instability.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted from referenced result graphs because the graphs and their numerical trajectories are absent from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Delay after training saturation, the chance-to-near-perfect jump, and dependence on training-set size. None is measured or reported numerically.
Critical dataset size, ungrokking, and circuit efficiency. The post only applies a norm penalty as an accelerator.

record.verdict_notes: This is an informal LessWrong post. The results plots were not supplied, and there are no seed counts, model details or dataset sizes. The reader's 'tests'/T2 and its V1 supports/limits_scope labels are not justified, because the rows are comparisons between methods.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test how grokking delay changes with training-set size. The supplied text does not give the accuracy trajectories needed to verify chance-to-near-perfect test accuracy or quantify the delay after training accuracy saturates.
No generalizing circuit, memorizing component, or continuous mechanistic progress measure is analyzed.
No non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale sweep, or weight-norm transition is tested.
No LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning is tested.
Although the method applies Frobenius-norm regularization, the post does not measure circuit efficiency, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below a dataset-size threshold.
The post does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.
No optimizer-instability or floating-point explanation is tested.
